title: Partial Orders and Hasse Diagrams
short: Draw a partial order such as "divides" as a Hasse diagram, and list the elements in an order that respects it.
trouble: Students draw the edges that transitivity already implies, or assume every two elements must be comparable.

blocks.html: Other relations behave like "comes before" or "is part of." Math Ladder itself is built on one: a topic can come before another because it is a prerequisite, and some pairs of topics simply have no order between them. Relations like that are partial orders.

A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. Examples: $\le$ on numbers, "divides" on positive integers, $\subseteq$ on sets. Two elements may be incomparable (neither is below the other). A Hasse diagram draws each element as a point, with $b$ above $a$ and an edge between them exactly when $a$ is below $b$ with nothing in between.

The Hasse diagram leaves out loops and every edge that transitivity already implies, and loses nothing. Reflexivity is automatic, so loops carry no information. And $a$ is below $c$ exactly when you can climb from $a$ to $c$ along edges, because each step up is a comparison and transitivity chains them. So the short list of "covering" edges encodes the whole relation, and the picture stays readable.

blocks.title: Drawing a Hasse diagram
blocks.q: List the edges of the Hasse diagram of the divisors of $12$ under "divides."
steps: Draw an edge from $a$ up to $b$ when $a \mid b$ and no divisor lies strictly between; for divisors this means $b/a$ is prime.
Edges: $1 - 2$, $1 - 3$, $2 - 4$, $2 - 6$, $3 - 6$, $4 - 12$, $6 - 12$. That is $7$ edges. The comparison $1 \mid 12$ is not drawn; it is implied by climbing $1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 12$.

blocks.title: Minimal and maximal elements
blocks.q: In $S = \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12\}$ under "divides," find the minimal and maximal elements.
steps: Minimal: nothing else in $S$ divides it. $2$ and $3$ qualify; $4$ does not ($2 \mid 4$).
Maximal: it divides nothing else in $S$. $8$, $9$ and $12$ qualify; $6$ does not ($6 \mid 12$).
A partial order can have several minimal and several maximal elements, because some elements are incomparable.

blocks.title: An order that respects the relation
blocks.q: Courses A, B, C, D, E have prerequisites: A before C, B before C, C before E, B before D. Give an order for taking all five.
steps: A course can be taken once everything below it is done. Start with the minimal ones: A and B.
After A and B, both C and D are available. After C, E is available.
One valid order: A, B, D, C, E. (Others work too, such as B, A, C, D, E.) Such an order is called a topological sort.
blocks.a: For example A, B, D, C, E

blocks.html: Drawing implied edges, or assuming every two elements are comparable. A Hasse diagram with an edge from $1$ straight to $12$ is cluttered and shows the relation poorly; that edge is already implied. And in "divides," $4$ and $6$ are incomparable: neither divides the other. Check: an edge $a - b$ belongs in the diagram only if nothing fits between; and before saying "the largest element," make sure it really is above everything.
